A mixed-studies systematic review was undertaken to enhance our understanding of sleep disturbances and mood disorders in women in late pregnancy and the postpartum period, their connection with breastfeeding, and the assessment of interventions for sleep disturbance. Three electronic databases (PUBMED, EMBASE and Google Scholar) were searched for qualitative, observational, and mixed-method studies from the year 2016 to June 2023. Twenty-nine articles were included in the analysis. The results were synthesized into four overarching themes: (і) the sleep quality of women in the perinatal period; (ii) the relationship between sleep and breastfeeding; (iii) the relationship between sleep quality and emotional disturbance in the perinatal period; (iv) sleep interventions in the researched group. Proper quality and quantity of sleep are essential for good health, well-being, and good overall quality of life. The perinatal and postpartum period is of great significance for women due to physiological changes, shifts in circadian rhythms, social setting, and psychological well-being, all of which affect the quality and quantity of their sleep. Sleep disorders in the perinatal and postnatal period may contribute to apathy, somnolence, tiredness, fatigue, low mood, anxiety, and a higher risk of depressive symptoms in the final stage of pregnancy and after childbirth.4,5 Sleep disturbances are a very sensitive indicator which allows to identify various mental illnesses, especially depression. There is a significant relationship between sleep disturbance, insomnia, and perinatal depression (antenatal and postpartum), which left untreated may have devastating effects on women, infants, and families, or even lead to maternal or newborn mortality.5 As circadian rhythm disorders frequently co-occur with sleep disorders and depression, many studies have investigated this cause-and-effect relationship.6 Is it enough for people predisposed to depression to experience long-term poor sleep quality and insomnia for their effects to add to the set of depressive symptoms and for depression itself to reveal? fetched_contents.text: Postpartum Thyroiditis What is postpartum thyroiditis? Postpartum thyroiditis happens when a person’s thyroid gland becomes inflamed within 1 year of delivering a baby or having a miscarriage or abortion. This condition affects a small percentage of pregnant people. The thyroid is a tiny, butterfly-like gland in the front of your neck. Its job is to make thyroid hormones. These hormones travel through your blood to all parts of your body. Thyroid hormones control how your body makes and uses energy (your metabolism). They affect almost every organ in your body. When your thyroid doesn’t make the right amount of hormones, you don’t feel well. Postpartum thyroiditis may first make your thyroid overactive (hyperthyroidism). This means it sends too many thyroid hormones out into the bloodstream. This can make parts of your body work too fast. But over time, the condition can lead to an underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism). This means it doesn’t make enough thyroid hormones. Then, parts of your body slow down, including your metabolism. Postpartum thyroiditis symptoms can also be attributed to postpartum depression or the stress of being a new parent. This is why it is important to see your healthcare provider for a diagnosis. What causes postpartum thyroiditis? Experts don’t know what causes this condition. But it is a lot like the autoimmune disease Hashimoto thyroiditis. It is hard to tell the 2 conditions apart. Who is at risk for postpartum thyroiditis? You may be more likely to get this condition if you have any of these: * Antithyroid antibodies before pregnancy * Type 1 diabetes * A history of thyroid problems * Family history of thyroid problems * Other autoimmune conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis, etc. What are the symptoms of postpartum thyroiditis? When the thyroid becomes inflamed, it first sends a lot of thyroid hormone into your blood. That causes hyperthyroidism. During this time, you may not have any symptoms. Or you may have any of the symptoms listed below under overactive thyroid. After this first phase, you may fully recover. Or your thyroid may be damaged. A damaged thyroid can become underactive. This condition may also go away. Or you may have an underactive thyroid for the rest of your life. In this case, you may need hormone replacement. Each person’s symptoms may vary. Symptoms may include: Overactive thyroid (hyperthyroidism) * Feeling warm or sweaty * Muscle weakness * Nervousness or anxiety * Fast heartbeat, palpitations * Loss of focus * Weight loss Underactive thyroid (hypothyroidism) * Extreme tiredness and lack of energy (fatigue) * Constipation * Memory loss * Feeling abnormally cold * Muscle cramps * Weakness * Weight gain These symptoms may not appear until a few months after childbirth. They may be mistaken for normal signs of recovery from childbirth. Always see your healthcare provider for a diagnosis. How is postpartum thyroiditis diagnosed? Tests used to diagnose postpartum thyroiditis depend on the phase of the disease. A blood test that measures thyroid hormone levels can often tell if you have an overactive or underactive thyroid. How is postpartum thyroiditis treated? Treatment will depend on your symptoms, age, and general health. It will also depend on how severe the condition is. Treatment depends on the phase of the disease and your symptoms: * Overactive thyroid. If you have major symptoms of hyperthyroidism, your healthcare provider will often prescribe beta-blockers. These medicines slow down your heart rate. * Underactive thyroid. If you have major symptoms of hypothyroidism, your provider will prescribe a thyroid hormone replacement called levothyroxine. You should have regular thyroid tests. Your thyroid may be working normally within 12 to 18 months after the symptoms start. If so, you may be able to stop treatment. Thyroid function will return to normal in 4 in 5 people. If you are in a high-risk group for developing postpartum thyroiditis, your provider may check for thyroid hormone abnormalities. They may do this 3 or 6 months after your delivery. Key points about postpartum thyroiditis * Postpartum thyroiditis happens when a p’s thyroid becomes inflamed after delivering a baby or having a miscarriage or abortion. It may first cause the thyroid to be overactive. But in time, it can lead to an underactive thyroid. * Experts don’t know what causes this condition. * You are more likely to get it if you had antithyroid antibodies before pregnancy. Other risk factors include having type 1 diabetes, a history of thyroid problems, or another autoimmune condition. * A blood test to check thyroid hormone levels can often tell if you have an overactive or underactive thyroid. * Treatment is based on how severe your symptoms are. Next steps Tips to help you get the most from a visit to your healthcare provider: * Know the reason for your visit and what you want to happen. * Before your visit, write down questions you want answered. * Bring someone with you to help you ask questions and remember what your provider tells you. * At the visit, write down the name of a new diagnosis and any new medicines, treatments, or tests. Also write down any new instructions your provider gives you. * Know why a new medicine or treatment is prescribed and how it will help you. Also know what the side effects are. * Ask if your condition can be treated in other ways. * Know why a test or procedure is recommended and what the results could mean. * Know what to expect if you do not take the medicine or have the test or procedure. * If you have a follow-up appointment, write down the date, time, and purpose for that visit. * Know how you can contact your provider if you have questions.

fetched_contents.text: Helping baby sleep through the night Newborns sleep 12 or more hours a day but just an hour or two at a time. Babies born before their due date, called premature, may sleep more than babies born at term. There may be no pattern at first. Babies wake up to eat and then fall back asleep. But after a couple weeks, babies will be able to stay awake longer, and then sleep for a longer time. A more regular sleep schedule comes with brain and nervous system growth and being able to go longer between feedings. After a few months many babies are on a regular three-times-a-day nap schedule and sleeping for longer periods at night. For caregivers, the age-old advice is "sleep when your baby sleeps. " While it's almost a cliche and sometimes impossible, getting enough sleep is as important for you as it is for your baby. In these first few months, caregivers often report that they are exhausted. Tired caregivers can find it hard to focus, remember details or see solutions to issues. Until you get into a new rhythm with your baby, it might help to set aside anything that doesn't have to be done. That way you have a better chance of getting the sleep you need. Every baby is different. But by age 3 to 4 months, many babies sleep at least five hours at a time. Babies this age should be sleeping around 12 to 16 hours a day including naps. And at some point during a baby's first year, babies will start sleeping for about 10 hours each night.

Evidence-based explanation of why sleep is so disrupted after childbirth

Sleep is disrupted after childbirth because the body is undergoing a major transition, and this affects sleep biology, caregiving demands, and physical recovery. The most authoritative evidence here is the systematic review on maternal sleeping problems before and after childbirth, which states that sleep disturbances are common in the perinatal and postpartum period and are influenced by physiological changes, shifts in circadian rhythms, social setting, and psychological well-being [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns cause young mothers to be vulnerable to sleep disorders, and that sleep disorders may progress to severe insomnia [N1-F1]. This matches the direct search evidence that postpartum insomnia is common and can be caused by postpartum hormones, including the drop in progesterone that facilitates relaxation [N1-R2].

Biological changes driving sleep disruption include hormonal shifts. The review explicitly says that sleep patterns may be altered by major hormonal, physiological, and behavioral changes experienced during pregnancy and after childbirth [N1-F1]. The hormone-related explanation is also supported by the evidence that postpartum insomnia is linked to hormonal changes and that sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies [N1-R1][N1-R2]. These hormonal changes can directly interfere with the body’s ability to regulate sleep, leading to insomnia and poor sleep quality [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Direct impacts of caring for a newborn on sleep continuity and duration are very clear in the evidence. The systematic review says that sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies, and that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns cause young mothers to be vulnerable to sleep disorders [N1-F1]. The Mayo Clinic practical guide reinforces this by explaining that newborns wake often to eat and then fall back asleep, and that caregivers often report exhaustion in these first few months [N4-F3]. This means that the newborn’s feeding and caregiving demands directly fragment sleep and reduce total sleep time, even though some studies show relatively stable total sleep time when daytime naps are included [N1-F1].

Postpartum physical recovery can also interfere with rest. The review states that sleep disturbances are sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression, and that sleep disorders in the perinatal and postnatal period may contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and a higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies [N1-F1]. While the evidence does not list a specific injury or pain condition in detail, it clearly links sleep disruption to postpartum fatigue and physiological recovery stress, suggesting that the body’s postpartum healing and physical demands reduce the capacity for restful sleep [N1-F1].

Overall, the strongest explanation is that postpartum sleep disruption is caused by a combination of hormonal changes, the newborn’s demands, and postpartum fatigue and recovery stress [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. The evidence is consistent across sources, though it is also limited in that the review notes subjective perception and the absence of an objective measurement tool [N1-F1]. That means the conclusions are plausible but should be interpreted as based on observational and self-reported data rather than a fully objective biological measurement [N1-F1].

Likely emotional and mental health drivers of overwhelm and low sleep

The evidence points to anxiety, depression, and burnout as likely drivers of overwhelm and low sleep in new parents. The systematic review on maternal sleeping problems before and after childbirth states that sleep disturbances are a sensitive indicator of mental illnesses, especially depression [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns can contribute to apathy, somnolence, tiredness, fatigue, low mood, anxiety, and a higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. Another source explicitly states that postpartum anxiety is characterized by excessive worry after childbirth and can manifest during pregnancy [N2-R2], while a review of motherhood and mental health identifies postpartum mood disorders, including postpartum depression, anxiety disorders, and psychosis, as impacting mental well-being [N2-R5]. This supports the idea that new parents can experience multiple overlapping emotional states rather than one isolated problem.

Common signs of anxiety, depression, or burnout in new parents include excessive worry, low mood, fatigue, anxiety, and difficulty concentrating [N1-F1][N2-R2]. The evidence also notes that postpartum depression may involve sadness, anxiety, and negative thoughts, and that it is linked to hormone imbalance [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The review on motherhood and mental health adds that postpartum mood disorders can range from mild to severe and can include anxiety disorders [N2-R5]. In terms of burnout, the evidence is more indirect, but the repeated theme of fatigue, exhaustion, and difficulty focusing in new parents supports the idea that prolonged caregiving strain can resemble burnout [N1-F1][N4-F3].

Lack of sleep worsens emotional regulation and overwhelm in a well-supported way. The systematic review says that sleep disturbances are sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression, and that sleep deficiency can lead to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep disturbances may contribute to apathy, somnolence, and tiredness [N1-F1]. This means that sleep loss does not just make someone feel tired; it can amplify irritability, anxiety, and difficulty coping with the demands of parenthood. The evidence also implies that poor sleep may make it harder to manage overwhelm because the emotional system becomes more vulnerable [N1-F1].

When postpartum mood symptoms may require clinical attention is clearly signaled by the evidence. The systematic review says that sleep disturbances may contribute to depressive symptoms and that untreated sleep disorders may have devastating effects on women, infants, and families [N1-F1]. The postpartum depression sources similarly state that postpartum depression starts after childbirth and includes symptoms such as sadness, anxiety, and negative thoughts, and that it is a mood disorder that may need treatment [N5-R2][N5-R3]. The evidence also emphasizes that symptoms can range from mild to severe and that postpartum depression has existed for as long as the condition itself [N5-R3][N5-R4]. That means that if a new parent experiences prolonged fatigue, persistent anxiety, sadness, or difficulty functioning, clinical attention is warranted rather than dismissing it as a temporary adjustment.

In summary, the evidence supports a clear chain: sleep loss worsens emotional regulation and overwhelm; anxiety, depression, and related mood disorders can appear as part of the postpartum experience; and when symptoms are severe, persistent, or interfere with daily life, professional help is appropriate [N1-F1][N2-R2][N5-R2][N5-R3][N5-R4].

Practical steps to improve sleep and reduce overwhelm

Practical sleep-hygiene strategies that are realistic for new parents include creating a calm nighttime environment, using a consistent bedtime routine, and managing nighttime caregiving demands. The evidence from the baby sleep guide says to follow a calming bedtime routine, put the baby to bed drowsy but awake, and use signs of tiredness as cues for bedtime [N4-R1]. The NHS advice adds that establishing a bedtime routine can involve a bath, night clothes, a fresh nappy, and bedtime story elements, and that staying calm and quiet at night is important [N4-R4][N4-R2]. The Mayo Clinic practical guide emphasizes that caregivers should sleep when the baby sleeps and that establishing a routine is important because tired caregivers can struggle with focus and problem-solving [N4-F3]. These strategies are realistic because they do not require perfect conditions but instead rely on small, consistent actions that can be adapted to a newborn’s irregular schedule.

Time-management and support strategies that can reduce fatigue include prioritizing essential tasks, accepting help from others, and using nighttime self-care. The Mayo Clinic evidence explicitly says that until a new rhythm is established, caregivers should set aside anything that doesn’t have to be done, which helps them get the sleep they need [N4-F3]. The nighttime self-care routine for new moms includes writing thoughts down, focusing on breathing, listening to something relaxing, putting the phone away, and keeping eyes off the clock [N4-R5]. These are practical steps because they address both the baby’s needs and the parent’s own capacity for rest without requiring major lifestyle overhauls. The evidence also underscores that fatigue can impair caregivers’ ability to focus and solve problems, making self-care especially important [N4-F3].

Signs that the family may need additional help or respite are not explicitly enumerated in the provided evidence, but the evidence does imply that prolonged exhaustion, difficulty concentrating, and ongoing sleep disruption are red flags. The systematic review states that sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies, and that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns can contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep disturbances may be sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression [N1-F1]. In practical terms, if a new parent is consistently exhausted, struggling to function, or feeling overwhelmed beyond what is expected, it may signal the need for respite or external support [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The evidence does not provide a formal checklist, so the strongest practical message is that persistent sleep loss and emotional strain should prompt a conversation about whether the family needs help rather than enduring it alone [N1-F1][N4-F3].

# Integrated patient-friendly answer on postpartum sleep and overwhelm

## 1) Why sleep is so disrupted after childbirth

The short answer is: this is normal in the early postpartum period, but it can feel overwhelming because of a mix of biological, caregiving, and recovery factors.

### Biological changes driving sleep disruption
The evidence shows that sleep is disrupted because childbirth triggers major changes in the body. A systematic review explains that sleep disturbances are common in the perinatal and postpartum period and are influenced by physiological changes, shifts in circadian rhythms, social setting, and psychological well-being [N1-F1]. It also says sleep patterns may be altered by major hormonal, physiological, and behavioral changes experienced during pregnancy and after childbirth [N1-F1]. Hormonal changes are especially important: one source notes that postpartum insomnia can be caused by the drop in progesterone, which helps relaxation [N1-R2]. So even if you feel exhausted, your body may be adjusting in ways that make sleep harder.

### Direct impacts of caring for a newborn
Caring for a newborn is a huge direct reason sleep is so disrupted. The same systematic review says sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies [N1-F1]. Another source explains that newborns often wake to eat and then fall back asleep, which can fragment sleep and leave caregivers exhausted [N4-F3]. This means that even if you’re trying to rest, your baby’s feeding and caregiving needs can keep you from getting enough continuous sleep.

### Postpartum physical recovery
Postpartum physical recovery can also interfere with rest. The review notes that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns can contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and a higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. So the body is not just recovering from childbirth; it’s also dealing with the added stress of recovery, which can make rest harder.

## 2) What is likely driving the overwhelm and low sleep

The evidence points to anxiety, depression, or burnout as likely drivers. The systematic review says sleep disturbances are sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep deficiency can lead to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. Other sources directly link postpartum anxiety to excessive worry after childbirth [N2-R2], while a review of motherhood and mental health identifies postpartum mood disorders including postpartum depression, anxiety disorders, and psychosis as affecting mental well-being [N2-R5].

### Common signs of anxiety, depression, or burnout
If you feel overwhelmed, it may be because of:
- excessive worry or anxiety [N2-R2]
- low mood, sadness, or negative thoughts [N5-R2][N5-R3]
- fatigue or tiredness [N1-F1]
- difficulty concentrating or problem-solving [N4-F3]
- trouble feeling calm or emotionally regulated [N1-F1]

### How lack of sleep worsens emotional regulation and overwhelm
The evidence is clear: poor sleep makes emotional regulation harder. Sleep disturbances are described as sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression [N1-F1]. Sleep deficiency can contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. In practical terms, if you’re already sleep-deprived, you may feel more irritable, anxious, or unable to cope with the demands of parenthood. That can make overwhelm feel even worse.

### When postpartum mood symptoms may require clinical attention
The evidence says that postpartum depression can start after childbirth and includes symptoms such as sadness, anxiety, and negative thoughts [N5-R2][N5-R3]. It also notes that symptoms can range from mild to severe and that postpartum depression has existed for as long as the condition itself [N5-R3][N5-R4]. The review on maternal sleeping problems similarly states that sleep disturbances may contribute to depressive symptoms and that untreated sleep disorders may have devastating effects on women, infants, and families [N1-F1]. So if your feelings are persistent, severe, or interfering with daily life, clinical attention is appropriate rather than dismissing them as just “baby blues.”

## 3) Medical conditions that could be mistaken for postpartum sleep issues

The evidence suggests that thyroid dysfunction can overlap with insomnia and anxiety, making it a medical condition that may be missed. Hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism have clinical overlap with sleep conditions such as insomnia, restless legs syndrome, and obstructive sleep apnea [N3-R1]. Postpartum thyroiditis can first make the thyroid overactive, with symptoms including nervousness or anxiety, fast heartbeat, loss of focus, weight loss, extreme tiredness, memory loss, feeling abnormally cold, muscle cramps, weakness, and weight gain [N3-F2]. It also notes that symptoms may be mistaken for normal signs of recovery from childbirth [N3-F2]. That means thyroid issues can mimic both insomnia and anxiety, and they may be missed without testing [N3-R3][N3-F2].

### Other medical causes
The evidence also points to hormonal insomnia and sleep apnea as possible overlaps. Hormonal insomnia can happen when hormone levels fluctuate or change [N3-R5]. Sleep apnea is mentioned in the overlap evidence as a condition that can co-occur with insomnia and other sleep disorders [N3-R1]. While the provided evidence does not give a detailed account of sleep apnea specifically in postpartum women, it does establish that sleep disorders can have overlapping medical roots [N3-R1][N3-F2].

### Why these conditions may be missed
The evidence strongly supports the idea that these conditions can be missed without testing. The thyroid evidence says symptoms can be mistaken for normal signs of recovery from childbirth and that it is important to see a healthcare provider for a diagnosis because the condition can be missed without proper testing [N3-F2]. It also states that the symptoms of thyroid disease overlap with hormonal changes, making a developing thyroid problem easy to miss [N3-R3]. That means if you’re experiencing insomnia, anxiety, fatigue, or mood changes after childbirth, a medical evaluation may be needed to rule out a treatable condition [N3-R1][N3-F2].

## 4) Practical steps to improve sleep and reduce overwhelm

The evidence supports several realistic strategies for new parents.

### Sleep-hygiene strategies
- Follow a calming bedtime routine [N4-R1]
- Put your baby to bed drowsy but awake [N4-R1]
- Establish a bedtime routine that may include a bath, night clothes, a fresh nappy, and bedtime story elements [N4-R4]
- Stay calm and quiet at night and try not to stimulate or wake babies when feeding or changing them [N4-R2]
- Keep nighttime routines consistent and realistic [N4-R3]

### Time-management and support strategies
- Sleep when your baby sleeps [N4-F3]
- Set aside anything that doesn’t have to be done until you get into a new rhythm [N4-F3]
- Use nighttime self-care routines, such as writing thoughts down, focusing on breathing, listening to something relaxing, putting your phone away, and keeping eyes off the clock [N4-R5]

### Signs that the family may need additional help or respite
The evidence does not provide a formal checklist, but it does imply that prolonged exhaustion, difficulty concentrating, and ongoing sleep disruption are red flags. The systematic review notes that sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies, and that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns can contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. In practical terms, if you’re consistently exhausted, struggling to function, or feeling overwhelmed beyond what is expected, it may signal the need for respite or external support [N1-F1][N4-F3].

## 5) Bottom line for you

You’re not alone in feeling overwhelmed and unable to sleep after giving birth. The evidence suggests that sleep disruption is common and is driven by a mix of hormonal changes, newborn caregiving demands, and postpartum recovery stress [N1-F1][N1-R2][N4-F3]. Emotional overwhelm and low sleep can also be linked to anxiety, depression, or burnout, and sleep loss can make those feelings worse [N1-F1][N2-R2][N5-R2]. At the same time, thyroid dysfunction and other medical conditions can mimic insomnia and anxiety, so it’s important to consider whether a treatable condition might be contributing [N3-R1][N3-F2].

If your symptoms are persistent, severe, or interfering with daily life, it’s reasonable to seek professional help rather than trying to manage everything alone [N1-F1][N5-R2][N5-R3]. For now, try to build small, realistic routines around sleep and self-care, and don’t hesitate to ask for help when needed [N4-F3][N4-R5].

In short: this is a common and often temporary period, but it’s also worth paying attention to so you can protect your health and your family’s well-being [N1-F1][N3-F2][N5-R2].

# Integrated patient-friendly answer on postpartum sleep and overwhelm

## 1) Why sleep is so disrupted after childbirth

The short answer is: this is normal in the early postpartum period, but it can feel overwhelming because of a mix of biological, caregiving, and recovery factors.

### Biological changes driving sleep disruption
The evidence shows that sleep is disrupted because childbirth triggers major changes in the body. A systematic review explains that sleep disturbances are common in the perinatal and postpartum period and are influenced by physiological changes, shifts in circadian rhythms, social setting, and psychological well-being [N1-F1]. It also says sleep patterns may be altered by major hormonal, physiological, and behavioral changes experienced during pregnancy and after childbirth [N1-F1]. Hormonal changes are especially important: one source notes that postpartum insomnia can be caused by the drop in progesterone, which helps relaxation [N1-R2]. So even if you feel exhausted, your body may be adjusting in ways that make sleep harder.

### Direct impacts of caring for a newborn
Caring for a newborn is a huge direct reason sleep is so disrupted. The same systematic review says sleep deficiency is common in postpartum mothers who feed and care for their babies [N1-F1]. Another source explains that newborns often wake to eat and then fall back asleep, which can fragment sleep and leave caregivers exhausted [N4-F3]. This means that even if you’re trying to rest, your baby’s feeding and caregiving needs can keep you from getting enough continuous sleep.

### Postpartum physical recovery
Postpartum physical recovery can also interfere with rest. The review notes that sleep deficiency, sleep interruption, and altered sleep patterns can contribute to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and a higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1]. So the body is not just recovering from childbirth; it’s also dealing with the added stress of recovery, which can make rest harder.

The evidence points to anxiety, depression, or burnout as likely drivers. The systematic review says sleep disturbances are sensitive indicators of mental illness, especially depression [N1-F1]. It also notes that sleep deficiency can lead to fatigue, tiredness, low mood, anxiety, and higher risk of depressive symptoms [N1-F1].
